ARTICLE OPEN Detailed immunophenotypic and genetic characterization of bone marrow clonal plasma cells and B-cells in early-stage monoclonal gammopathies

Oihane Pérez-Escurza 1,2, P. Martijn Kolijn3, Jón Þórir Óskarsson 4,5, María González-González1,2,6, María Jara-Acevedo1,2,6,7, Julio del Pozo1, Quentin Lécrevisse 1,2,6, Juan Flores-Montero 1,2,6,8, Luzalba Sanoja-Flores9, Silvia Martín1, Elín Ruth Reed4, Stephen Harding9, Sigrún Thorsteinsdottir 4,10, Sæmundur Rögnvaldsson4,11,12, Thorvardur Jon Love4,13, Brian Durie14,16, Anton W. Langerak 3, Sigurdur Yngvi Kristinsson 4,15, Alberto Orfao 1,2,6✉, on behalf of the iStopMM* and ECRIN-M3*

© The Author(s) 2026

Monoclonal gammopathy (MG) of undetermined signiﬁcance (MGUS) is the earliest and most prevalent stage of MG that may progress to symptomatic multiple myeloma (MM) or Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM) through intermediate smoldering forms of both diseases. We used next-generation ﬂow cytometry (NGF) to identify and purify bone marrow (BM) clonal plasma cells (cPC) and B-cells/lymphoplasmacytic cells (cB-cells) from 25 asymptomatic individuals with MG diagnosed within the population-based iStopMM screening program for further molecular analysis by next-generation sequencing (NGS). IgM-MGUS cases consistently exhibited WM-like phenotypes by NGF, and MYD88 p.L265P and/or CXCR4 mutations in the coexisting cPC and cB-cells. Conversely, cPC from non-IgM MGUS and smoldering MM (SMM) displayed a MM-like phenotype associated with genetic drivers –i.e., t(11;14)–, frequently coexisting with genetically unrelated cB-cells. Interestingly, recurrent RUNX1 single nucleotide variants were detected in cPC, but not coexisting cB-cells, from WM-like cases, suggesting a role for RUNX1 in PC differentiation. In summary, NGF enabled detailed immunophenotypic characterization of BM cPC and cB-cell populations in all cases analyzed, subdivided in IgM vs non-IgM cases with WM-like or MM-like phenotypic and genetic proﬁles, respectively. These ﬁndings underscore the potential contribution of NGF and NGS for accurate classiﬁcation or early-stage disease, beyond conventional criteria.

INTRODUCTION Monoclonal gammopathy (MG) of undetermined signiﬁcance (MGUS) is the most prevalent clonal plasma cell (PC) neoplasm, an asymptomatic condition that precedes malignant (symptomatic) PC diseases such as multiple myeloma (MM) or Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), via the intermediate smoldering MM (SMM) and smoldering WM (SWM) stages, respectively [1–4]. Population-based screening studies revealed a frequency of MGUS of ≈3.2–5% among adults older than 50 years (y), depending on the method used to detect a serum monoclonal (M)-component, i.e., serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) followed by conﬁrmatory immunoﬁxation (IF) or mass spectrometry (MS) [5–8]. Among MGUS, IgM-MGUS typically progresses to SWM and WM (or non-WM non-Hodgkin lymphoma), and rarely to IgM-MM [3, 9–11]. In contrast, non-IgM MGUS and light-chain MGUS more

frequently evolve to SMM and MM [4]. Since WM and MM represent disease conditions that display different clinical features and require distinct management approaches and therapeutic interventions, a clear-cut differential diagnosis between both entities already at the earliest e.g., MGUS stages becomes of utmost clinically relevance. At present, discrimination between both disease entities at the MGUS stage is not accurate and it mainly relies on the immunoglobulin (Ig) heavy-chain isotype of the secreted M-component (i.e., non-IgM vs IgM), combined with cytomorphological and/or histopathological assessment of the bone marrow (BM), including enumeration of clonal PC (cPC) alone and together with presence of ( > 10%) lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrates in SWM vs MGUS, respectively, in the absence of organomegalies and organ dysfunction (i.e., CRAB criteria: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, bone disease) [4, 12].

In recent years, next-generation ﬂow cytometry (NGF) has emerged as a highly sensitive technique for detecting clonal PC, B-lymphocytes and lymphoplasmacytic cells in patients with MG, both at diagnosis and following therapy [13, 14]. In addition, NGF has conﬁrmed the occurrence of uniquely different immunophe-notypes of cPC, clonal B-cells and/or lymphoplasmacytic cells (cB-cells) in SMM/MM (CD19−CD38lo CD45−/lo CD56−/+ CD117−/+ cPC without clonally-related B-cells) vs SWM/WM (CD19+ CD45+

CD56− CD117− cPC coexisting with clonally-related CD19+

CD20+ CD22lo CD25+ B-cells). The latter cB-cells can also be clearly differentiated from (CD5+ CD20lo CD23+) cB-cells typically found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)-like (or other less frequently non-CLL-like) monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) cases [14–20]. The clonal nature of phenotypically aberrant cPC and cB-cells can be further conﬁrmed by the restricted expression of Ig light chain kappa (κ) or lambda (λ) in the cytoplasm (cy) and/ or the cell surface (s) membrane of the suspicious cPC and cB-cell populations, respectively [19, 20]. Despite distinct aberrant immunophenotypic patterns have been described for cPC and/ or cB-cells in SMM and MM vs SWM and WM, systematic phenotypic and molecular characterization of these populations at the precursor non-IgM MGUS and IgM-MGUS stages remains incomplete, particularly among non-IgM MGUS and IgM-MGUS cases with coexisting (genetically related and unrelated) cPC and cB-cells. Here, we investigated the clonal relationship between coexisting cPC and cB-cells, together with the occurrence of recurrent MM- vs. WM-associated genetic alterations in BM of a subgroup of (otherwise) healthy adult donors included in the Iceland Screens, Treats, or Prevents MM (iStopMM) program [21], who showed the presence of a serum M-component. Our main goal was to characterize the immunophenotypic and molecular patterns of cPC and/or cB-cells and to assess the utility of NGF for a more accurate diagnostic classiﬁcation of MG, already at the earliest MGUS stages identiﬁed among subjects from the general population via diagnostic screening programs. In addition, we aimed at in-depth analysis of the genetic landscape of the puriﬁed compartments of coexisting BM cPC and cB-cells to identify molecular proﬁles that might contribute to the differential accumulation of genetically-related cPC vs cB-cells, already at the earliest stages of WM-related diseases.

MATERIALS AND METHODS Patients and samples A total of 25 individuals (13 women and 12 men; median age of 68 years, ranging from 48 to 86 years) selected from a cohort of 75 individuals which had been consecutively diagnosed with a MG without prior history of a lymphoproliferative disorder, previously evaluated by next-generation ﬂow cytometry (NGF) within the Iceland Screens, Treats, or Prevents Multiple Myeloma (iStopMM) study [21], were enrolled in this substudy. iStopMM is a nationwide, population-based screening study from Iceland in which adult ( ≥40 years) volunteers are being screened for serum and/or urine M-protein, with positive cases undergoing further evaluation, including PB and BM sampling. These 75 individuals correspond to participants from whom paired BM and PB samples were obtained, which were subsequently analyzed by NGF for the identiﬁcation and characterization of clonal B-cell and/or PC populations between September 2019 and December 2022. From this cohort, a subgroup of 25 subjects was selected for this study according to the following criteria: (1) presence of a serum M-protein by high-sensitive capillary zone electrophoresis and/or an altered free Ig light chain (FLC)-ratio (The Binding Site, Birmingham, UK); associated with, (2) ≥1 clearly deﬁned population of cPC coexisting or not with ≥1 population of cB-cells as identiﬁed by NGF; and, 3) availability of ﬂuorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-puriﬁed BM cPC and/or cB-cells for further molecular analyses. Following the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) diagnostic criteria [1], cases were classiﬁed as MGUS (n = 19) and SMM (n = 6). The remaining cases could not be included due to the absence of detectable clonal populations and the inability to reliably purify enough number of clonal B-cells due to limited sample availability after the

NGF analyses and/or very low clonal B-cell/PC inﬁltration levels. Paired EDTA-anticoagulated bone marrow (BM) aspirated samples (2 mL) and peripheral blood (10 mL) specimens from each donor were collected in Iceland and sent to the University of Salamanca (Salamanca, Spain) for sample processing within 36 h, as described elsewhere [22, 23]. All subjects enrolled in this study provided their informed consent to participate according to the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Icelandic National Bioethics Committee (NCT03327597), and the Icelandic Data Protection Agency. Permission for transfer of all biological samples for this study (Registration number: 2020/252) was granted by the Spanish Ministry of Health.

Immunophenotypic studies For immunophenotypic identiﬁcation, characterization and puriﬁcation of cPC and other coexisting cB-cell populations, the EuroFlow 2-tube 8-color NGF-MM minimal residual disease (MRD) antibody panel and the Lymphocyte Screening Tube (LST) were used to stain BM samples (Suppl. Table 1), as previously described [22]. Stained samples were measured in FACSCantoTM II or FACSLyricTM ﬂow cytometers –Becton/Dickinson (BD) Biosciences, San Jose, CA–, and data was analyzed with the InﬁnicytTM

software (v2.1.a.000; BD-Cytognos, Salamanca, Spain) as detailed elsewhere [22].

Puriﬁcation of individual populations of clonal plasma cells and B-cells and extraction of genomic DNA Populations of cPC (n = 28) and cB-cells (n = 20) were puriﬁed from BM samples, after they had been stained with a panel of antibodies directed against cell surface membrane markers, using a BD FACSAriaTM III instrument (Cell Sorting Service, University of Salamanca, Spain). A median (range) number of 60,000 (900–1,300,000 cells) cPC with a median purity of 98%, and of 40,000 (500-8,000,000 cells) cB-cells with a median purity of 99% (assessed only in samples with > 5000 cells isolated), were collected. Genomic (g) DNA was extracted from the FACS-sorted cells using the QIAamp® DNA micro kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) as per the manufac-turer’s instructions.

IGHV gene sequencing and identiﬁcation of recurrent MM-related and WM-associated genetic alterations An IGHV leader-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay was used to identify IGHV sequences of puriﬁed (paired) cPC (n = 10) and cB-cells (n = 14) from a subset of 10/25 cases (7 MGUS and 3 SMM), and to establish the clonal relationship among those clonal cell populations coexisting in the same sample. For this purpose, the leader-based IGH variable (V) region clonal rearrangement NGS assay (Leader assay), and the EuroClonality-NGS Working Group standard operating procedures (SOP) were used, as described elsewhere [24]. Brieﬂy, ampliﬁcation of IGHV gene rearrangements was performed using the IGHV leader primer set, including 24 forward primers directed at the IGHV leader sequences and a single reverse primer designed against a conserved IGHJ sequence [24], for a one-step polymerase chain reaction (PCR). PCR products were then pooled in an equimolar (4 nM) solution into two separate multiplexed library pools for cPC and cB-cells, to avoid cross-contamination. Paired-end sequencing (2 × 300 pb) was performed on an Illumina MiSeqTM sequencer using the MiSeq reagent v3 kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA). Sequencing data were analyzed using the ArresT/Interrogate platform (EuroClonality-NGS Working Group) for accurate clonotype identiﬁcation, as previously described [25]. The clonal relationship between cell populations from the same sample was established by direct comparison of the dominant clonotype sequence (i.e., identical IGHV–IGHD–IGHJ junctional regions) together with identical complementarity determining region 3 (CDR3) sequences across the different cell compartments derived from individual BM samples. Clonotypes with low read counts or below variant-allele frequency (VAF) thresholds ( < 3%) were considered non-informative and excluded from those analyses. Due to technical limitations and/or insufﬁcient amount of gDNA, this analysis could not be performed on the remaining FACS-puriﬁed cPC (n = 18) and cB-cells (n = 6) gDNA samples. The presence of recurrent MM- and WM-associated genetic alterations was investigated in gDNA from FACS-puriﬁed cPC (n = 23) and cB-cells (n = 16) from 25/25 study cases (19 MGUS and 6 SMM) following the EuroClonality-NGS DNA capture assay and SOP [26] for detection of chromosomal translocations/gene fusions, somatic gene mutations and IGH, IGK and IGL gene rearrangements associated with lymphoid neoplasms [26]. Among MGUS cases, BM biopsy systematically showed PC inﬁltration levels of ≤10% at diagnosis ( ≤5% in 7/19 and 6–10% in 9/19 cases). In the remaining 3/19 cases, BM samples were of poor quality for reliable histopathological assessment; however, complementary BM cytomorphologic and ﬂow cytometry data showed cPC levels of 6% and 1%, respectively, whereas it could not be quantiﬁed in the third case. These results were associated with low serum IgM (n = 7), IgG (n = 8) and IgA (n = 4) M-protein concentrations –median (range): 3 g/l (0–8.9 g/l)–. In turn, the majority of patients newly diagnosed with SMM in parallel to the MGUS cases (4/6) displayed between 11 and 15% PC in their BM biopsy with > 15% BM PC levels in the other 2/6 cases, together with greater median (range) serum M-protein concentrations of 13.5 g/l (0.4–15.8 g/l) (Suppl. Table 2).

High-sensitive immunophenotypic studies and ﬁnal diagnosis NGF analyses identiﬁed coexisting cPC and cB-cells in BM of 15/25 (60%) of cases including 12/19 MGUS and 3/6 SMM patients. In contrast, the remaining 17/25 individuals exhibited an immunophenotypic proﬁle consistent with MM-like cPC alone, or cPC coexisting with ≥1 phenotypically unrelated cB-cell populations resembling low-count CLL-like or non-CLL-like MBL. Based on those NGF results, hereafter cases were regrouped as 12 non-IgM MGUS, 5 SMM and 8 WM-like MGUS cases (IgM-MGUS plus IgG/ IgM SMM) (Suppl. Table 3).

DISCUSSION NGF immunophenotyping has emerged as a key tool to improve the classiﬁcation of early-MG, through high-sensitive identiﬁcation and characterization of the underlying cPC and/or cB-cell populations [22]. While immunophenotypic proﬁles of these clonal cell populations are well-established in overt (symptomatic) MM and WM patients, comparative data related to the earliest disease stages, particularly non-IgM or IgM-MGUS, still remain limited. Here, we investigated the utility of NGF for the identiﬁcation and characterization of BM cPC and/or cB-cells present in (otherwise healthy and asymptomatic) adults with early-stage MG identiﬁed through the population-based iStopMM screening program in Iceland [21]. In addition, we assessed the contribution of NGF to improving disease classiﬁcation and validated immunophenotypic ﬁndings through NGS analysis of puriﬁed clonal cell populations, targeting recurrent genetic alterations associated with MM, WM and other related mature B-cell neoplasms [27–31]. BM cPC and/or cB-cell populations were immunophenotypically assigned to either an MM-like or WM-like disease proﬁles [22]. Notably, phenotypic stratiﬁcation by NGF revealed that all IgM-MGUS individuals and one SMM case with biclonal IgG plus IgM serum M-components, unequivocally exhibited an WM-like immunophenotypic proﬁle, and was more likely to be classiﬁed within the spectrum of WM-like neoplasms [16, 32]. As expected, this reassignment was supported by the demonstration of identical IGHV and IGK/IGL rearrangements between coexisting cPC and cB-cells, together with MYD88 p.L265P and/or CXCR4 gene mutations consistent with the genomic landscape of WM [27, 30, 33–37]. The reassignment of the SMM case into the WM-like group is particularly noteworthy given the distinct biological trajectories and clinical implications of both entities [38, 39]. Together, these ﬁndings underscore the relevance of the speciﬁc cell driving MG based on immunophenotypic and molecular features, rather than relying exclusively on conventional diagnostic criteria. In contrast, cPC and (when present) coexisting cB-cells, from non-IgM MGUS/SMM cases displayed immunophenotypic proﬁles consistent with MM-like disease and harbored recurrent MM-related genetic alterations, most commonly IGH translocations, –i.e., t(11;14)–, without MYD88 or CXCR4 mutations [40, 41]. Importantly, in non-IgM MGUS/SMM cases where coexisting cB-cell populations were detected in addition to cPC, these typically exhibited a CLL-like (and less frequently a non-CLL-like) MBL phenotype, associated with unrelated IGHV and/or IGK/IGL gene rearrangements between cPC and cB-cells, conﬁrming that they most likely represent independent neoplastic cell compartments, rather than belonging to a single evolving clone. Although coexistence of clonally unrelated B-cell and PC populations has been only sporadically reported [42, 43], population-based studies have shown that CLL-like MBL clones are frequently detectable in (otherwise) healthy adults using high-sensitive NGF [44, 45]. Thus, the presence of minor clonal B-cell populations in individuals with MM-like cPC on immunophenotypic grounds should not be interpreted per se, as evidence of an underlying lymphoplasmacytic disorder, but rather as a risk factor for lymphoid malignancy development [46]. Our observations are also aligned with recent clinical evidence showing that approximately 10% of MGUS cases from the iStopMM study present with multiple paraproteins, most of them being transient, and some of them displaying more than one aberrant cPC population, suggesting coexistence of biologically independent processes, rather than linear clonal evolution [47]. Interestingly, recurrent genetic alterations, including both t(11;14) in cPC (with high median VAF) from nearly half of

non-IgM MGUS and more than half of SMM cases, and MYD88 p.L265P mutation (with median VAF of 44%) in both cPC and cB-lymphocytes of WM-like MGUS cases, were detected at both high frequency and high variant allele burden in early-stage disease. These ﬁndings indicate that such alterations likely arise early during clonal ontogeny and may act as initiating events driving disease development, being detectable at high VAF, not only in the terminally differentiated cPC, but also in upstream precursors such as the coexisting cB-cell populations in WM-like MGUS cases [35, 36, 48, 49]. In contrast, in one of our CXCR4-mutated WM-like cases, MYD88 p.L265P was detected exclusively in the cB-cell compartment at low VAF (i.e., 13%), while absent in the remaining CXCR4-mutated cPC fraction, potentially reﬂecting a MYD88 mutational burden below the detection threshold in cPC in an individual where the CXCR4 mutation could represent the driver genetic event, as discussed below [27]. Beyond those potential (recurrent) genetic drivers, we further identiﬁed a complex landscape of shared and/or cell compartment-restricted genetic alterations, even in cases with clonally related cPC and cB-cell populations. Most interestingly, recurrent RUNX1 mutations were identiﬁed exclusively in the cPC compartment of WM-like cases, while absent in their coexisting cB-cells, despite clear evidence of a common origin of both clonal cell populations. Although recurrent RUNX1 mutations were identiﬁed exclusively in the cPC compartment, and they have not been previously reported in WM and SWM, RUNX1 is known to be upregulated during B-cell differentiation toward plasmablasts and PC, its disruption delaying this transition in MM [50]. Our ﬁndings would suggest that RUNX1 mutations may promote PC differentiation from the cB-cell precursor population, thus contributing to the disease evolutionary proﬁle, already at early stages of WM disease (i.e., IgM-MGUS with a WM-like proﬁle) rather than clonal initiation [34, 50]. Notably, despite two translocations involved chromosome 2, only one affected the IGK locus. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst report of a IGK gene translocation in WM-like MGUS patients, though translocations involving the IGL gene locus in chromosome 22 have been sporadically reported in WM [31]. The remaining alterations were identiﬁed as being restricted to a single clonal B-cell or PC compartment and were largely non-recurrent, reﬂecting i) subclonal heterogeneity in WM-like cases, and ii) the absence of clonal relationship between cPC and the coexisting (independent) cB-cell populations in non-IgM MGUS/ SMM cases [35, 37]. In this regard, CXCR4, ATM and TP53 mutations were detected in both cPC and cB-cell compartments of WM-like cases [51, 52]. Of note, CXCR4 mutations, typically considered to be subclonal, and acquired after MYD88 p.L265P, were usually detected at lower frequency and VAF, consistent with prior reports, except for the one case discussed above, where CXCR4 emerged as the primary genetic event [35, 37, 53, 54]. Conversely, cPC-restricted mutations showed a more heterogeneous distribution, including PTPRD and speciﬁc IGH translocations in WM-like cases, RUNX1 in non-IgM MGUS and SMM, and CREBBP in SMM. In non-IgM MGUS cases with cPC only, mutations in ATM, NRAS, DIS3, H1-2 and/or H1-3, as well as high-risk IGH translocations, were identiﬁed. Likewise, transition to an earlier disease stage should not be directly interpreted as true biological regression, but rather a reclassiﬁcation based on the evaluation of a single BM aspirated sample in the context of a low tumor burden, which may highlight the potential inaccuracy in some patients, of single histopatho-logic and cytomorphologic BM assessments for diagnostic purposes, underscoring the need for approaches that minimize reliance on isolated measurements and/or provide more accurate quantiﬁcation of BM cPC and cB-lymphocytes. Further studies in larger patient cohorts followed for longer periods are needed to accurately establish the rate of progression of our cases compared to other patients included in the iStopMM program. Despite the selection criteria signiﬁcantly reducing sample size from the initially available cohort due to the requirement of sufﬁcient numbers of FACS-puriﬁed clonal B-cells and PC for downstream molecular analyses, thereby introducing a degree of selection bias towards cases with higher clonal burden, all included cases originate from a population-based screening setting and therefore remain representative of the earliest stages of MG. In summary, our results show that even with a limited sample size, NGF enabled detailed characterization of cPC and cB-cells in early-stage MG, revealing substantial biological heterogeneity even among MGUS cases identiﬁed through population-based screening. Integration of NGF, cell sorting and NGS conﬁrms the presence of MM-like and, particularly, WM-like driver genetic alterations already at the earliest stages of the disease and reveals compartment-speciﬁc genetic complexity, any conclusion about its relative frequency requiring further studies in larger patient cohorts. Importantly, NGF-based classiﬁcation reﬁned diagnostic accuracy in around one-quarter of our cases, compared to conventional criteria alone, which supports its role as a complementary frontline diagnostic tool for MG.
